snippet: Hi everyone, We are green-lit for the Q3 platform migration. The goal is to move the ingestion pipeline and the reporting service off the legacy cluster before the end of September
subject: Q3 platform migration - kickoff and open questions
to: Demo User <demo@example.com>, Theo Reyes <theo.reyes@example.org>, Ines Calder <ines.calder@example.com>, Rafael Kim <rafael.kim@example.org>
bodyText:
Hi everyone,

We are green-lit for the Q3 platform migration. The goal is to move the ingestion pipeline and the reporting service off the legacy cluster before the end of September, with no customer-visible downtime.

I have blocked two hours on Thursday for a kickoff. Before then, I would like each of you to write down the three things that worry you most about your own area. We will start from those instead of from a happy-path plan.

Rough shape of the plan as I see it today: dual-write for four weeks, shadow reads for two, then a cutover per tenant starting with the smallest accounts.

-- 
Maya Oberon
Head of Platform
maya.oberon@example.com

snippet: Thanks Maya. My three worries, in order: 1. The ingestion pipeline still writes directly to the legacy schema in two places (the backfill job and the manual replay tool). Dual-writ
subject: Re: Q3 platform migration - kickoff and open questions
to: Demo User <demo@example.com>, Maya Oberon <maya.oberon@example.com>, Ines Calder <ines.calder@example.com>, Rafael Kim <rafael.kim@example.org>
bodyText:
Thanks Maya. My three worries, in order:

1. The ingestion pipeline still writes directly to the legacy schema in two places (the backfill job and the manual replay tool). Dual-write does not cover those, so a cutover would silently drop rows.

2. We have no reliable way to compare shadow reads. The reporting service rounds differently on the new cluster, so a naive diff reports thousands of false positives.

3. Nobody owns the rollback path. If a tenant cutover goes wrong at 3am, I do not know who is allowed to flip it back.

None of these are blockers, but all three need an owner before we start dual-writing.

-- 
Theo Reyes
Staff Engineer - Ingestion
theo.reyes@example.org

What I cannot do alone is the billing-plan migration. That needs someone who understands the historical pricing rules, and honestly that is only Rafael.

subject: Orbital Weekly newsletter
bodyText:
Issue 41 - The cost of a fast build

Build times are a team-size problem - A ninety-second build feels free to the person who wrote the change and expensive to the team of thirty waiting behind it. This week we look at three teams that measured the queue instead of the build.

Caching is not free either - Every cache you add is a new way to be wrong. Two engineers describe the week they spent chasing a bug that was a stale artifact the whole time.

Reader question: when to stop optimising - Our answer, unsatisfying as ever: when the next hour of work saves less than the hour costs, measured over a quarter rather than a sprint.

You are receiving this because you signed up for Orbital Weekly. Unsubscribe or manage your email preferences at example.org.

snippet: Issue 42 - Migrations that finished Six migrations, five survivors - We asked six teams that completed a platform migration what they would do differently. Five said the same thing
subject: Orbital Weekly newsletter
bodyText:
Issue 42 - Migrations that finished

Six migrations, five survivors - We asked six teams that completed a platform migration what they would do differently. Five said the same thing: decide the rollback owner before writing any code.

The dual-write trap - Dual-writing is easy to start and hard to stop. The teams that finished had a written definition of done for the old path, not just the new one.

Shadow reads deserve a tolerance - Exact comparison sounds rigorous and produces noise. Every successful shadow-read setup we found had a tolerance and a documented reason for it.

snippet: Issue 43 - Reviews, batching, and interruption Why your fastest reviewer is your slowest - Reviewer assignment by file history concentrates work on the people who already know the
subject: Orbital Weekly newsletter
bodyText:
Issue 43 - Reviews, batching, and interruption

Why your fastest reviewer is your slowest - Reviewer assignment by file history concentrates work on the people who already know the code, which is exactly the group with no spare hours.

Two windows a day - Batched reviews consistently beat continuous ones in the data we collected, but only where the team agreed on the windows in advance.

The shallow-review risk is real - Speed gains are easy to measure and quality losses are not. If you batch, pick a signal for depth before you start.

subject: Orbital Weekly newsletter
bodyText:
Issue 44 - Saying no to a twenty-four-month discount

Long contracts price your uncertainty - A two-year discount is cheap only if you know your usage profile. Several readers wrote in about paying for a tier they outgrew in month four.

Burst pricing, honestly assessed - Burst pricing works when your bursts are rare and real. If you burst every month, that is not a burst, that is your baseline.

Negotiating without a bluff - A migration threat you would not carry out costs you the next three negotiations. Two procurement leads explain what they say instead.

subject: Orbital Weekly newsletter
bodyText:
Issue 45 - Permissions that expire

Temporary access is permanent access - Unless revocation is a scheduled job rather than a calendar reminder. This is the single most repeated piece of advice we have published.

Narrow roles beat broad ones - A role that can flip exactly one flag is easier to grant widely and safer to forget about than a role that can do everything.

What we got wrong last week - Our build-queue maths in issue 41 assumed serial builds. Three readers corrected us, and they were right.
